title: Build and deploy AI at the edge for real-world impact | OD837

segments.text: COSMOS DARWIN: Hello,
and thanks for tuning into Microsoft Build.
My name is Cosmos Darwin.
I'm a Product Manager on the Microsoft Azure team.
In this session, we're going to be talking
about shipping physical AI to the edge using a variety
of technologies for Microsoft's Adaptive Cloud approach,
including Foundry Local and Azure Local.
Now, here's specifically what we're going to cover.
First, I want to take just a moment to, sort of,
frame the opportunity and the challenges of physical AI.
We talk a lot about AI, including this week
at Microsoft Build, but often, it's in the context
of a chatbot on a computer screen.
There's so much more potential than that when we talk
about bringing AI out into the physical world.
That's what we'll frame
up as the opportunity for this session.
Then I'll show a demo of a basic agentic robot
to help you understand the opportunity
for combining language models and generative AI
with physical systems.
Then we'll spend most of the session unpacking how it works.
I want to really give you a sense for some
of the core ideas, what's novel and what isn't relative
to conventional robotics.
Then, finally, I'll just very briefly mention a few
of the Adaptive Cloud technologies that we used
in this demo including small form factor infrastructure,
Foundry Local enabled by Azure Arc,
and the Azure IoT Operations suite of platform services.
Now, this session is for builders, so I'm not going
to give you the marketing pitch for each of those products,
but I do just want to give you a sense for how we used them
to put together the basic agentic robot that we showed.
Without any further ado then, let's get started.
What is physical AI?
Well, when we talk about AI, we talk a lot
about the transformative potential, how AI helps
so many people to really achieve more, to do things
that they might have thought before would take a long time.
Suddenly, that time is compressed and things
that you would have considered to be a large,
challenging task can be completed very quickly,
but the benefits from those advancements have not been
evenly distributed.
An awful lot of the examples we give are documents
or spreadsheets, basically, information workers benefiting
from the advances of AI.
Let me give you a few examples of types of work
that have not really seen that same change.
For example, performing inspections or maintenance
or even repairs out in the physical world.
This work has not really benefited from the advances
of AI in the last few years.
Similarly factories yeah
you can automate manufacturing in a factory context.
A lot of things are actually built outside of a factory.
You can look around and you'll see job sites everywhere
where construction is happening,
and you won't see a lot of robots.
It's people performing that work.
Similarly, in logistics and distribution and warehousing,
a lot of this looks the same now as it did a decade
or even two decades ago.
Those gains in productivity have not really materialized yet.
Those things, once they get distributed through logistics
and arrive at brick-and-mortar retail
or quick-serve restaurants, a lot of the work
of stocking shelves or food prep, similarly,
has not really benefited from this advancement with AI
in the last few years.
There's a common theme to all of these examples,
which is that in each of these situations,
interacting with other people and interacting
with a changing environment around you, with changes
in the open world, is a core part of the work.
This is something
that historically robots have struggled with.
Robots excel when you're in a controlled environment,
you're doing the exact same task over and over,
so a factory is a great example of this,
but all of those examples I just gave are domains
where robots have struggled to make inroads.
As a result, the work looks an awful lot
like it has for decades.
However, what's exciting is that many people, myself included,
believe that that is beginning to change.
With some of the advances in recent years with AI models
and being able to run them locally, it is possible to go
from robotics to a more agentic approach to robots
that may be better able to do a lot of these tasks.
To illustrate that, my team
and I have put together a basic example.
Now, let me set expectations.
This robot I'm about to show you, it's not going
to take anyone's job, but it does serve to sort
of show the potential of combining AI,
especially language models, with physical systems.
Take a look.
[ Music ]
Hey, robot, can you pick up the red cube?
[ Music ]
That's right and put it in the bowl.
[ Music ]
Wait, I changed my mind.
Can you give it to me?
[ Music ]
Thank you.
Now pick up the green brick.
[ Music ]
Now put it in this green bowl.
[ Music ]
That's right.
Well done.
Isn't the robot cute?
[Laughter] Now look, as I said, it's a simple
or a basic example, so that robot is not about to go
out into the open world and address any
of the scenarios I talked about at the beginning, but I do want
to reflect on a few
of the interesting aspects of what we just saw.
I, as the person interacting with the robot, did not need
to adhere to a strict syntax of commands to sort
of start or stop the robot.
I could interact with it
in a very natural way, in a very fluid way.
I could just say what I wanted it to do,
even if it was a kind of rambling sentence.
"Hey, robot, please, would you mind maybe picking
up that thing there?"
The robot, because it's an agentic robot, is able to reason
about what it heard and figure out what I meant anyway,
even though the interaction was kind of messy, the inputs coming
from a person were messy.
Likewise, it was able to respond as the environment
around it changed, because it's continuously listening,
continuously looking, and when I moved objects on it
or when I changed the instruction midstream,
it was able to sort of pick up and adapt and keep going.
You can easily imagine a version of that
with a different embodiment, more sophisticated hardware,
for example, with more different things that it knows how to do,
being a helpful collaborator in spaces where, historically,
people have not been able to benefit
from having a helpful robot collaborator
because of the challenges I mentioned.
Okay. How does it actually work?
Let's unpack a little bit, what is going on behind the scenes
in that demo, so that you can see the pieces that are new
and novel and then the other pieces which, actually,
are very much just sort of conventional robotics.
Everything you saw in the demo, all of the intelligence required
to make the robot work as shown,
runs on this small, industrial computer.
For the demo, we use the Lenovo ThinkEdge SE100
because it's sort of industrial grade.
It has an optional NVIDIA discrete GPU,
but many other devices would work too.
This is just the one that we chose.
This computer is physically on the table,
co-located with the robot.
You can see it actually in the background of the video,
and it's connected just over USB, nothing fancy,
to three peripherals: First, a UVC-compliant RGB camera,
which is positioned over the workspace looking
down at the table.
Second, a UAC-compliant omnidirectional microphone,
which, of course, is used to capture the speech.
Then finally, the small tabletop robot arm, which has six degrees
of freedom and a seventh if you want
to count the gripper attachment that it has.
By the way, all of these are deliberately approachable,
off-the-shelf budget options,
because there's very little preventing you
from just trying this at home yourself, as we did.
Now in the video, you can see each of these things,
but just to sort of show you clearly, that was the USB camera
over the work surface, and that's the USB microphone.
These really are -- there's nothing terribly fancy
about these.
It's not a depth camera or anything like that.
It's just a classic, almost like a webcam,
so that's the hardware setup.
Perhaps a little more interesting is
on the software side.
On that small form factor industrial computer,
we chose to run the Azure Linux operating system,
and then Foundry Local, which you may know as something
that was originally available on Windows, then it expanded
to Windows and Android.
Foundry Local is now newly packaged as a container image
that you can run on Linux, which was a great fit
for our scenario here.
Foundry Local then hosts all of the AI models that we use
to make the robot do what it does.
At runtime, here's how this actually comes together.
Firstly, audio from the microphone is split
into utterances, and then fed into Nemotron Speech Streaming.
Nemotron is a speech-to-text model
that was developed by Nvidia.
It's available for free
in the Foundry Local catalog, and it's great.
It's one of the best models in terms of performance
and in terms of very low error rate.
As you saw in the video, even though I am facing away
from the microphone, not speaking terribly clearly,
there's a bunch of ambient noise, it was still able to pick
up and transcribe everything I said very reliably.
Feeding the audio into Nemotron Speech gives us back text
of what was said by the user.
In parallel with that, frames from the camera
over the work surface are continuously being captured
and fed into a variety of vision models,
including an open vocabulary detector model,
to recognize everything that we can see on the surface.
That certainly includes colored blocks and the little bowls
or containers that we put them in.
It includes a human hand, for example,
but it's not limited to that.
Something we didn't show in the video is, also,
just everyday objects can be recognized
by these detector models, so sunglasses, for example,
or a wedding ring, that's no problem.
It will pick them up.
Basically, for each of these detections,
it's returning the coordinates within the frame
of where that object was seen.
As applicable, it also returns the orientation, the major axis
of rotation, because, of course, that's very important
if the robot is going to go actually pick that object up.
The vision pipeline gives us these coordinates
and angles of rotation.
Now for the most important part, the reasoning.
All of these inputs, the text from the speech pipeline
and the coordinates from the vision pipeline,
are fed into a small language model that runs locally
on that small industrial computer.
Now for the demo, we chose Quen3 because it's available for free
in the Foundry Local catalog, and it supports reasoning
and tool calling, but many other options would likely work
as well.
We chose the 1.7-billion parameter version,
which most people would say means it's a small language
model, but if you had more compute available,
you could also run a larger version
and quite possibly handle more complex types of instructions.
What's happening here is given all of the inputs,
the language model is asked to choose between a set
of tool calls that are available to it.
Now, for our example, again,
it's very basic, it's very simple.
We just gave it four tools that it knows how to call.
Those tools are Pick, so go pick up an item at a location.
Place, put it somewhere at some other location, or Pick
and Place, all as one movement.
Then the final tool call is Stop.
When it hears something like in the video when I say "Wait,"
it interprets that as a "Stop" tool call.
All the language model does is decide based on what it sees
and hears, which of these tools is it being asked to call?
In the example we've been using, of course,
it's a pick-and-place tool call where the
"Pick" target is the red cube; the "Place" target is the hand,
me, and once it has done that interpreting,
the rest is pretty straightforward, right?
That gets converted into a sequence of movements
that get planned out and then the robot arm executes them.
This part is really no different
from how it would have been in the past.
What's so interesting is the additional flexibility,
the additional almost humanness that comes
from the robot being able to interpret very messy inputs
and still figure out what you meant and then complete the task
if it's among the set of tools that it has.
All right.
There were a number of adaptive cloud technologies that we used
to make this demo possible, and so I do want
to just briefly touch on each of them.
The first one is the small form factor infrastructure,
that industrial computer that we use to run the whole demo.
There are a bunch of capabilities
that Microsoft Azure has offered for several years
that have previously been limited
to Azure Local on big servers.
This is things like provisioning machines from the cloud
or managing them from the cloud.
What's new is that those capabilities are now available
in preview for these smaller industrial form factors,
so take a look.
In the Azure portal, I can go provision a machine.
You'll see when I input the ownership voucher
for that Lenovo SE100 that I have, it picks it up,
and I can actually choose what software stack to install
onto this computer straight from the cloud portal without needing
to plug in a keyboard or monitor.
In this case, I chose Azure Linux, and I could do
that provisioning entirely from the cloud.
Once I do that, I get a resource representation
in the Azure Resource Manager for this computer.
You'll see it looks and works an awful lot
like a cloud virtual machine.
It's a provisioned machine resource type,
and it has a bunch of things that I get visibility into
and management functions that I can perform.
One simple example is I can grant access to this machine
to a colleague of mine directly
from the cloud portal using Microsoft Entra ID,
which means I don't need to have a password on a Post-it note
that I've written down or SSH key that I send to them.
This is a much more robust way of managing a device like this,
which is going to be really important if I want
to take this system and have hundreds or thousands
of them distributed across many locations.
Being able to manage it all
through the cloud control plane is going
to be extremely helpful.
That's one of the things that we did in this demo.
Another one which I've already mentioned is we used Foundry
Local, and specifically, the flavor of Foundry Local
that is newly available now as a container image for Linux.
On our small form factor industrial computer,
we installed Azure Linux as I said.
Now also to keep all of this straight,
we also just installed K3s, like a small, single-node Kubernetes,
and then we packaged our application code as a container.
That code is just Python.
It's really not terribly fancy.
Alongside that container, we then deployed Foundry Local
in a container, and Foundry Local exposes an open AI
compatible REST API that we can use
to make inferencing requests, and this is great
because it means we don't need to host the AI models
in our own code, which can be very clunky.
It can kind of -- you can run into challenges related to size
and agility and all sorts of reasons
that you don't really want to do it that way, but also,
there are a few specific advantages to this approach
that I thought were pretty compelling.
The first is Foundry Local gives you a trusted, authoritative way
to access a safe instance of a model.
In our demo, we wanted Quen3,
the 1.7-billion parameter version.
All we had to do was give its name in our configuration file
and then Foundry Local goes out and retrieves a trusted copy
of that model from the Foundry Local online catalog,
downloads it to run entirely locally, and from that point on,
there are no calls to the cloud at all.
It's just running inside of that Foundry Local container for you.
You can see in the catalog here,
there are so many options available,
including Nemotron Speech, the other model
that we used in the demo.
Once the model is running,
you can then just access it using an endpoint very much the
way you would if it was running in the cloud.
It's like a drop-in replacement
for making an API call to a public cloud.
Instead of accessing, say, Azure to run the model,
the model is running locally
on the small form factor device right next to your code.
What's great about that, of course,
is the latency is super predictable, and for a system
that is going to be out in the physical world interacting
with people, it all needs to be as close to real time
as you can get, so this is a great fit.
Now speaking of real time, the other thing
that Foundry Local takes care
of that I loved is it handles detecting the available hardware
accelerators in your hardware and lighting them up for you.
In our case, our Lenovo SE100 has an Nvidia GPU.
It has an RTX 2000 in it, and when you're using Foundry Local
on top of the small form factor infrastructure managed
through Azure, the whole top-to-bottom stack can be lined
up for you.
Everything from the kernel mode driver to the device plug-in,
to the user mode libraries that are inside
of the Foundry Local container, all of that is lined up.
Actually, as you see in the diagram,
your own application code doesn't even need to do anything
with the GPU, actually.
You're still benefiting from GPU-accelerated inference,
because as you make those inference requests
to Foundry Local, they happen much quicker
because the GPU is there.
In this instance, it sped up reasoning by Quen
by a factor of many times.
We tried it both ways.
This was a huge boost.
Here you can actually see a screenshot.
This is a pre-release tool,
so it may change a little before we release it,
but you can see a screenshot of that Nvidia RTX 2000E running
in our device, and in the Azure portal,
I can see the usage of that GPU.
Every time Quen is asked to interpret some instructions,
you can see a small spike in the GPU usage,
which shows you that it's being used.
All right.
The last piece of the puzzle I want to talk
about is Azure IoT Operations.
IoT Operations is a suite of platform services
that enables you to connect to devices and protocols
in your local environment.
Then connect the data from them up into the cloud,
and potentially, route commands back, such as mission plans
for a robot, for example.
IoT Operations includes a number of built-in connectors
that are really handy for things like OPC UA, HTTP, ONVIF,
and it also includes an industrial grade MQTT broker
that you can configure so that as data flows into the broker,
you can then configure how it gets transformed and sent
up to the cloud, for example,
for you to do analysis in Microsoft Fabric.
Now in our example, there are some things
that we were interested in monitoring.
One of them is the robot's span or reach, right?
Our robot, of course, is very small, and it can only reach,
I don't know, maybe half a meter or something.
The field of view of the camera is actually larger than that,
and so occasionally, you have the situation
where the camera can see an object, and the robot believes
that it's being asked to go pick or place that object,
but it actually can't reach it, as you see in this image here.
Now, in the case of just a single robot on a tabletop,
of course, it's not that hard to diagnose this yourself,
but you can imagine deploying this
across many locations in the field.
Being able to get real-time telemetry and intelligence off
of a system like this is everything.
That is where Azure IoT Operations is so valuable.
Let me show you.
On the K3 instance that we run
on this small industrial computer,
we deployed Azure IoT Operations using the extension approach.
Both IoT Operations and Foundry are available as extensions,
which means it's just a couple of clicks or a single YAML file,
and you're off to the races.
Once IoT Operations is installed,
you get this really approachable operations experience,
which would be usable not only by a more IT persona,
but actually an operations persona
who maybe has specific knowledge
about millimeter offsets and things like that.
You can configure how data should flow
from a discovered asset in your environment, in this case,
the robot arm, up into a workspace in the cloud,
and you can even transform that data here.
For example, if you needed to do a unit conversion or add
or remove additional properties, like in our example,
we're just trying to see if the coordinates are safe to reach.
For example, we could remove the z-coordinate,
because it doesn't really matter here.
You can do that through this very approachable interface,
so that when the data arrives in Microsoft Fabric,
it's ready for your data team to just interact with.
It's already cleaned up.
It's already formatted in a way that they'll understand.
For us, we configured Azure IoT Operations to stream all
of the coordinate requests from the robot.
Every time that it is asked to go grab something
at a particular location,
it streams back what coordinates it was asked to grab from,
and we can then analyze if those were safe or unsafe.
All of that is coming in real time off of the system,
so you can imagine if you were going to deploy this broadly,
this would be an extremely valuable capability.
Okay. Where does that leave us?
Advances in AI together
with Azure's Adaptive Cloud approach are making it easier
than ever to build and operate intelligent physical systems.
This year and I think in the years ahead, we are going
to have to update our notion of what types
of tasks it is possible to extend AI
to with an agentic approach to robotics.
If you're as excited about this as I am, I encourage you
to get started right now.
All of the things that we showed here are available off the shelf
for you to try.
The small form factor infrastructure is available
in preview now.
You can take it for a spin.
Foundry Local as a container image for Linux,
enabled by Azure Arc, is also available
as a preview right now.
You can go try that out for a scenario like ours
or many other scenarios as well.
Of course, last but not least,
Azure IoT Operations is also available for you to try.
All right.
That's it for me.
Thank you so much for watching and enjoy the rest of Build.
